reasons:
**Yes.**

A business is generally presumed to have greater sophistication and familiarity with insurance practices and risk disclosure than an individual householder, so courts and insurers reasonably expect businesses to proactively disclose material facts even absent specific questioning.

**Yes.**

A business, especially one engaged in commercial transactions, is generally expected to have greater sophistication and knowledge regarding risk disclosure in insurance dealings, and courts often impose a higher duty of good faith disclosure on commercial entities because they are presumed to better understand what facts are material to the insurer's risk assessment, even when the insurer's application doesn't specifically ask about that fact.

**Yes.**

Businesses are generally presumed to have greater sophistication and knowledge regarding risk disclosure in commercial transactions, so courts and insurance law often impose a higher duty of disclosure on them (even absent specific inquiry) than on ordinary individual consumers, who are typically only required to answer the questions actually asked.

**Yes.**

A business, being more sophisticated and knowledgeable about risks relevant to its own operations, is generally expected to exercise a higher degree of care and disclosure in commercial transactions like insurance underwriting than an ordinary individual householder, who is presumed to have less expertise in identifying what facts might be material to an insurer.

**Yes.**

A business is generally expected to have greater sophistication, access to professional advice, and awareness of what facts are material to an insurance contract, so the law reasonably imposes a higher duty of disclosure on it than on an ordinary householder who cannot be expected to know what matters to an insurer absent being asked.

**Yes.**

A business is generally presumed to have greater sophistication and knowledge regarding risk-related facts relevant to insurance, so the duty of disclosure (utmost good faith) is often applied more rigorously to commercial insureds than to ordinary consumers, who are protected by the expectation that insurers will ask about matters they consider material.

**Yes.**

A business is generally expected to have greater sophistication and knowledge regarding risk-related facts material to its operations, so courts and insurers reasonably impose a higher duty of disclosure on commercial insureds than on ordinary individual householders, who may not even recognize a fact's materiality.

**No.**

The duty of disclosure in insurance law generally turns on what a reasonable insured would consider material and what the insurer chose to ask about, not on whether the policyholder is a business or an individual—if the insurer's questionnaire did not prompt disclosure of the fact, the insurer bears the risk of its own failure to ask, regardless of the insured's commercial sophistication.

**Yes.**

A business is generally expected to have greater sophistication and awareness of what facts are material to an insurance risk, so the law (and good faith duty in insurance contracts) typically imposes a higher duty of disclosure on commercial entities than on ordinary individual householders, who are presumed to have less insurance expertise and may reasonably rely more heavily on the insurer's questions to identify relevant facts.

**Yes.**

A business is generally expected to have greater sophistication, access to professional advice, and familiarity with insurance practices than an individual householder, so the law reasonably imposes a higher duty of disclosure on commercial applicants even regarding facts the insurer failed to specifically ask about.
